notes: Lease consent appeal; structural alteration and shop front construction issues are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Unreasonable withholding of consent to restaurant alterations
key_facts: Tenants under a long lease at 4 Risborough Lane sought consent to convert ground floor premises into an Indian restaurant.
Landlords refused consent to structural alterations including removal of load-bearing piers and insertion of a new front door.
The county court recorder declared consent had been unreasonably withheld and granted declarations permitting the works.
Expert evidence showed the architect's plans did not specify what would happen if load-bearing walls were found on site.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Canterbury County Court declarations that landlords unreasonably withheld consent to structural alterations under clause 3(h) of the lease.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declarations discharged; landlords reasonably refused consent because tenants had not sufficiently specified proposed alterations affecting structural integrity and exterior main wall.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tenant seeks consent to structural alterations, the landlord may reasonably refuse if the tenant's plans leave material uncertainty about load-bearing features; a landlord is not required to grant conditional consent, and the shop front in this lease did not include the exterior main wall so consent to a new door in that wall was not required to be tested for reasonableness.
legal_issues: Principles governing reasonableness of withholding consent to structural alterations
Whether refusal based on structural concerns was reasonable
Construction of demise including shop front and exterior wall
Whether conditional consent should have been given

Tollbench Ltd v Plymouth City Council [1988] 1 EGLR 79

notes: Solicitors' disciplinary appeal; penalty reduction and Langford approach are clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor's suspension reduced after inadvertent child video undertaking breach
key_facts: Mr Chohan, a solicitor with mainly civil experience, signed a CPS undertaking while on his feet in the magistrates' court without realising it was an undertaking.
He authorised a trainee to copy a video recording of a child witness interview in a serious sexual offence case.
The Solicitors' Disciplinary Tribunal found conduct unbefitting and imposed six months' suspension.
The child witness's identity had not entered the public domain and the tribunal made no finding of dishonesty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under the Solicitors Act 1974 against penalty imposed by the Solicitors' Disciplinary Tribunal after admission of breach of undertaking.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; suspension set aside and replaced with a financial penalty of £2,500; Law Society ordered to pay the appellant's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Following the Langford approach after the Human Rights Act, an appellate court may substitute its own penalty where the breach of undertaking was unintentional and involved no moral turpitude; suspension was disproportionate in these exceptional circumstances despite the gravity of breaching undertakings protecting child witnesses.
legal_issues: Appropriate appellate standard after Langford and Ghosh
Whether six months' suspension was proportionate
Whether breach involved lack of integrity, probity or trustworthiness
Distinction between deliberate and inadvertent breach of undertaking

Langford v Law Society [2002] EWHC (Admin) 2802

notes: Attorney General's reference on racially aggravated wounding; sentence increase and AG reference principles clear.

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient sentence for racially aggravated neck wounding increased
key_facts: Brett Charlton pleaded guilty to racially aggravated wounding after slashing a 16-year-old black youth across the neck with a knife at Worthing station.
The offender used racist language and caused a wound requiring 18 stitches near vital structures.
Judge Thorpe indicated in chambers that a section 20 plea might avoid further custody to allow a Drug Treatment and Testing Order to continue.
The judge sentenced Charlton to 10 months' imprisonment and later had to impose three years for an earlier burglary when probation refused a DTTO.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 following a guilty plea and 10-month sentence for racially aggravated wounding.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to refer granted; sentence increased to three years' imprisonment, comprising two years for the wounding and one year for racial aggravation, to run from the date of the court's order.
enrichment.ratio: A judicial indication before plea does not preclude an Attorney General's reference where prosecution did not acquiesce in the lenient course; racially aggravated violence must be punished severely and the sentence should transparently reflect both base wounding and racial aggravation.
legal_issues: Effect of judicial sentence indications on Attorney General's references
Whether prosecution acquiescence barred the reference
Appropriate sentence for racially aggravated wounding on a guilty plea
Impact of judge's focus on drug treatment on sentencing

notes: Complex restitution contribution appeal; subrogation and full indemnity outcome are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Negligent certifier indemnified by bank that paid away mistaken letter-of-credit funds
key_facts: Niru paid about US$5.8 million under a letter of credit backed by a negligent SGS inspection certificate and a fraudulent FIATA bill of lading in a lead ingot sale.
Credit Agricole received the funds from Bank Sepah but paid them away to Mahdavi's group in bad faith after selling the underlying goods.
SGS satisfied the joint judgment against it and CAI while CAI paid nothing.
Moore-Bick J held SGS entitled to full recovery from CAI by subrogation despite earlier draft views of equal blame.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal in contribution proceedings between Credit Agricole and SGS following joint judgment in favour of Niru and Bank Sepah.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; SGS entitled to recover the full principal and interest it paid to Niru from CAI by equitable subrogation and recoupment.
enrichment.ratio: Where a restitution defendant paid away money received under a mistake in bad faith, satisfying a joint judgment by a negligent tortfeasor entitles that tortfeasor to full indemnity by subrogation because CAI remained unjustly enriched and would have had no liability if it had acted in good faith and repaid the funds.
legal_issues: Whether SGS was entitled to subrogation against CAI
Whether recoupment principles applied between tort and restitution defendants
Whether the 1978 Act permitted contribution between tortfeasor and restitution defendant
Relative responsibility of SGS and CAI for Niru's loss

notes: Inter-country adoption and section 20 freeing-order appeal; split judgments but appeal dismissal clear.

enrichment.short_title: Unlawful inter-country adoption placement did not revive freeing-order rights
key_facts: Four children of Mr and Mrs B were freed for adoption after extreme parental misconduct including abduction from foster care.
Birmingham City Council placed two children abroad with prospective adopters without prior section 55 authority, breaching section 56.
Two children later returned to foster care in England while two remained abroad with Mr and Mrs A.
Parents applied under section 20 to revoke freeing orders for the children placed abroad.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Permission to appeal treated as appeal against dismissal of parents' section 20 applications to revoke freeing orders.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted but appeal dismissed; section 20 applications in relation to C and T rightly dismissed, though placement breached section 56.
enrichment.ratio: Although a local authority's placement of freed children abroad without section 55 authority breached section 56, an unlawful placement can still be a placement for adoption within section 20(1)(b), so parents' revocation rights did not revive; alternatively a later section 55 order defeated the application.
legal_issues: Whether inter-country placement without section 55 authority breached section 56
Whether an unlawful placement satisfied section 20(1)(b)
Construction of Schedule 2 paragraph 19 of the Children Act 1989
Effect of a subsequent section 55 order on section 20 rights

enrichment.short_title: Iranian asylum appeal adjourned over overlooked torture medical evidence
key_facts: Mohamed Shihab Mazrae, an Iranian national, failed before an adjudicator and the Immigration Appeal Tribunal to establish asylum entitlement.
Credibility findings turned partly on limited medical evidence about loss of a testicle and alleged torture in detention.
A Dr Browell report, not fully weighed below, supported the applicant's account of severe beatings and possible trauma-related surgery.
Permission to appeal had been refused on limited grounds excluding the expert-report challenge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision dismissing an asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application adjourned on notice to the Secretary of State with appeal to follow immediately if permission granted; listing before three Lord Justices for half a day.
enrichment.ratio: Where important evidence may have been overlooked at earlier stages, a court may adjourn a permission application rather than finally refusing it, applying the principle in E and R that reopening requires a risk of serious injustice because of something that went wrong or important evidence overlooked.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred in excluding the expert-report ground
Whether overlooked medical evidence created a risk of serious injustice
Scope of permission limited to ethnicity and illegal departure grounds
Application of E and R v Secretary of State principles

notes: Attorney General's reference on false imprisonment; court declined to increase unduly lenient community sentence.

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient false imprisonment sentence left undisturbed on reference
key_facts: A 46-year-old lodger pleaded guilty to false imprisonment of his landlady after breaching bail conditions following earlier assaults in her home.
He locked her in the house for about an hour, threatened to kill her, put a knife to her throat and was subdued with a Taser after she escaped.
Judge Machin imposed a 100-hour community punishment order and two-year community rehabilitation order despite about ten weeks in custody.
Psychiatric evidence indicated bereavement-related mental illness, remorse and low risk of similar reoffending.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging an unduly lenient non-custodial sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to refer granted, but the court declined to increase the sentence because of double jeopardy, progress on the community order and exceptional mitigation.
enrichment.ratio: Although a community sentence for this false imprisonment was unduly lenient and a starting point of about three years would ordinarily have been appropriate, the Court of Appeal will not lightly interfere where the judge had a proper basis including out-of-character conduct and psychiatric evidence of low risk, especially given double jeopardy and partial completion of the community order.
legal_issues: Whether the community sentence was unduly lenient
Aggravating effect of breach of bail and use of weapons
Role of psychiatric mitigation and out-of-character conduct
Whether the court should exercise its discretion not to interfere despite unduly lenient sentence

notes: Fabric copyright infringement action; copying inference and secondary infringement findings are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Pineapple fabric design indirectly copied by imported Luxor cloth
key_facts: Nouveau Fabrics claimed copyright in Nigel Thompson's stylised pineapple motif design for furnishing fabric sold from 1993.
Voyage imported Luxor fabric from Italy via Sotexport; the motif was strikingly similar though woven differently.
The Italian provenance evidence was inconsistent and failed to rebut an inference of copying from publicly available Pineapple fabric.
Both defendants continued dealing after letter before action without adequately investigating the copying allegation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial of copyright infringement claims for secondary importation and sale of allegedly infringing fabric.
enrichment.outcome: Copyright infringement found against Voyage and Dunelm from 8 February 2002; damages to be assessed separately.
enrichment.ratio: Close similarity between an original artistic motif and an imported fabric, combined with weak and inconsistent evidence of independent creation and failure to investigate after notice, supports inference of indirect copying; a defendant has reason to believe articles are infringing copies when enquiries fail to provide a credible innocent explanation.
legal_issues: Whether Luxor copied a substantial part of the Pineapple artistic work
Inference of copying from similarity and access
Whether defendants knew or had reason to believe copies were infringing
Application of Designers Guild v Russell Williams similarity principles

notes: Rolled-up holiday pay appeal; Working Time Directive analysis and Scottish divergence clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: Rolled-up holiday pay held compatible with Working Time Directive
key_facts: Workers in Caulfield had collectively agreed continental shift arrangements with 13.36% rolled-up holiday pay in hourly rates.
Mr Clarke's CIS contract specified daily pay including a separate holiday element but paid nothing during actual holiday.
The EAT held specified rolled-up arrangements could satisfy regulation 16 if a definite sum or percentage was allocated to holiday pay.
The Inner House in MPB Structures Ltd v Munro had reached the opposite conclusion on Article 7.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals against Employment Appeal Tribunal decisions on lawfulness of rolled-up holiday pay under the Working Time Regulations and Directive.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed in principle; Caulfield contracts held lawful and Clarke remitted on factual issues; court indicated a reference to the Court of Justice was appropriate.
enrichment.ratio: Article 7 does not require holiday pay to be paid at the time leave is taken; contractual rolled-up pay with a specified allocation is not an impermissible obstacle to paid annual leave where workers retain genuine entitlement to leave and payment, especially under collectively negotiated terms.
legal_issues: Whether rolled-up holiday pay violates Article 7 of the Working Time Directive
Whether payment must be associated with the taking of leave
Effect of MPB Structures Ltd v Munro on English tribunals
Construction of regulations 13, 16 and 35 of the Working Time Regulations

Gridquest Ltd [2002] ICR 1206
